purpose: Decitabine is used to treat a blood and bone marrow disorder called myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), which is a condition where your bone marrow does not make enough healthy blood cells. It helps slow down the disease and can reduce the need for blood transfusions. Your doctor may also use it for certain types of leukemia.
how_it_works: Inside your body, cancer cells have certain 'switches' that are turned off, preventing normal cell behavior. Decitabine works by turning those switches back on so that abnormal cells can either behave more normally or stop growing. It does this by blocking a chemical process called methylation, which is like removing a lock that was keeping healthy genes silenced.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include low blood cell counts (which can cause fatigue, increased risk of infection, and easy bruising or bleeding), nausea, constipation, diarrhea, fever, and swelling in your hands or feet. You may also feel very tired during treatment.
warnings: Because decitabine lowers your blood cell counts, you are at a higher risk of serious infections and bleeding — call your doctor right away if you have a fever, unusual bruising, or signs of infection. This medication can harm an unborn baby, so reliable birth control is very important for both men and women during treatment and for a period of time afterward. Tell your doctor about all medications you take, including vitamins and supplements.
typical_dosing: Decitabine is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) in a clinic or hospital setting, typically over 1 to 3 hours. A common schedule is once daily for 5 days in a row, with the cycle repeating every 4 weeks. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule based on your specific condition and how your body responds to treatment.
